narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 55.2% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your class ranking at the end of your third year was the strongest influence and pushed the prediction toward failure. Being in the second decile is substantially lower than the average of roughly sixth decile among students who were accepted, signaling weaker long-term academic performance in law school.

Your undergraduate GPA of 3.70 worked in the opposite direction. This is noticeably higher than the 3.23 average of accepted students, so the model saw it as a meaningful reason you might still pass the bar. Your LSAT score of 37 was almost exactly at the accepted-student average and therefore had only a modest favorable pull.

Taken together, the model concluded that your relatively low third-year ranking outweighed the positive signals from your strong college grades and solid LSAT, tipping the scales just past the acceptance threshold.

What you should do next is straightforward: focus on improving your academic standing in the remaining years of law school. Raising your class rank would directly address the factor that hurt your application the most and would likely change future predictions in your favor. Consider speaking with your academic advisor about targeted steps to climb in the rankings before you sit for the bar.
